subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Count the City
hook: Help Arjun and Priya explore their city and understand how large numbers describe the world around them!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious 12-year-old who loves exploring his city

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Arjun's smart classmate who notices numbers everywhere

slides.title: A Mystery in Numbers
slides.storyContext: On a Saturday morning, Arjun and Priya explore their Delhi neighborhood. They see a banner: Welcome! Population: 16 million! Arjun asks, What does 16 million even look like?
slides.inSimpleWords: Arjun and Priya wonder about very big numbers.

image.alt: A Mystery in Numbers — Large Numbers Around Us

slides.title: Ones, Tens, Hundreds
slides.storyContext: Priya pulls out her notebook. Let me show you, she says. She writes: 1, 10, 100, 1000. Each step multiplies by 10! Like building blocks stacked higher and higher.

points.label: Place Value
points.text: 1 (one), 10 (ten), 100 (hundred), 1,000 (thousand)

example.problem: Write 5 hundreds and 7 tens and 3 ones.

slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers build up by tens, like stairs.

image.alt: Ones, Tens, Hundreds — Large Numbers Around Us

slides.title: Thousands and Lakhs
slides.storyContext: They reach a market. Look! says Arjun, pointing at a sign: ₹15,000 — Laptop Price. Priya writes: 1,000 = one thousand. 1,00,000 = one lakh. Indian rupees use lakhs!

points.label: Indian Place Value
points.text: 1,00,000 = 1 lakh. We group by 2s after hundreds: 1,00,000; 10,00,000 = 10 lakh; 1,00,00,000 = 1 crore

example.problem: How many lakhs are in 25,00,000?
example.solution: 25 lakhs

slides.inSimpleWords: India uses lakhs and crores for big money.

image.alt: Thousands and Lakhs — Large Numbers Around Us

slides.title: Counting the Crowd
slides.storyContext: A festival starts in the park. Look at all these people! says Priya. A volunteer says: Last year, 2,50,000 people came to this festival! Arjun's eyes widen. 2 lakh 50 thousand?

points.label: Reading Large Numbers
points.text: 2,50,000 = 2 lakhs and 50 thousands

slides.inSimpleWords: Big festivals have hundreds of thousands of visitors.

image.alt: Counting the Crowd — Large Numbers Around Us

slides.title: Comparing Large Numbers
slides.storyContext: A news report shows: Delhi has 1,60,00,000 people. Mumbai has 2,04,00,000. Arjun compares on his fingers. Priya says, Mumbai is bigger by 44 lakhs!

points.label: Comparing
points.text: Line up digits from right. Compare place by place, left to right.

example.problem: Which is bigger: 5,67,890 or 5,76,890?
example.solution: 5,76,890 is bigger because 7 ten-thousands > 6 ten-thousands

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare number sizes by checking digit positions.

image.alt: Comparing Large Numbers — Large Numbers Around Us

slides.title: A Billion Stars
slides.storyContext: At an astronomy show, the guide says: Our Milky Way has 1,00,00,00,000 stars - 1 billion! Priya writes: 1,00,00,00,000 = 1 crore x 100. Arjun gasps. Thats... bigger than our city!
slides.inSimpleWords: A billion is 100 crores - way bigger than cities.

image.alt: A Billion Stars — Large Numbers Around Us

slides.title: Arjun and Priya's Discovery
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Arjun and Priya sit in the park. Priya says: Numbers describe everything - cities, crowds, stars, even time! Arjun smiles. From ones to billions, numbers are everywhere!

points.label: Key Takeaway
points.text: Place value: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, lakhs, crores, billions. Each shift right multiplies by 10.

slides.inSimpleWords: Large numbers describe the world around you.

image.alt: Arjun and Priya's Discovery — Large Numbers Around Us

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Solve the Festival Budget
hook: Help Arjun and Priya plan a school festival by solving arithmetic expressions!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A practical 12-year-old helping organize a school event

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: The smart mathematician ensuring calculations are correct

slides.title: Planning the School Festival
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya are asked to budget for the annual school festival. The principal says: Food costs 3,000, decorations cost 2,000, and prizes cost 1,500. What's the total? Priya writes: 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add costs to find the total budget.

image.alt: Planning the School Festival — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Order of Operations (BODMAS)
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Arjun: We follow BODMAS - Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. Always in that order! She writes: 2 + 3 x 4. Not 5 x 4 = 20. But 3 x 4 first = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

points.label: BODMAS Rule
points.text: Do Brackets first, then Orders (powers), then ÷ and ×, then + and −. Work left to right for equal priority.

example.problem: Solve: 10 + 2 × 3
example.solution: 2 × 3 = 6 first. Then 10 + 6 = 16

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply and divide before adding and subtracting.

image.alt: Order of Operations (BODMAS) — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Brackets Matter
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: What if I calculate (3 + 2) × 4? Priya nods. Brackets first! 3 + 2 = 5, then 5 × 4 = 20. Different from 3 + 2 × 4 = 3 + 8 = 11!

points.label: Brackets
points.text: Solve inside brackets first. (3 + 2) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20

example.problem: Which is bigger: (2 + 3) × 5 or 2 + 3 × 5?

slides.inSimpleWords: Brackets are calculated first.

image.alt: Brackets Matter — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Solving the Budget Puzzle
slides.storyContext: A vendor offers: Buy 10 samosas at ₹5 each, or 20 at ₹4 each. Buy 2 of each offer! Priya writes: (10 × 5) + (20 × 4) = 50 + 80 = 130. Arjun checks her work. Perfect!

points.label: Real-world expressions
points.text: Food budgets need careful calculation with brackets and multiplication.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use math to plan real festivals and costs.

image.alt: Solving the Budget Puzzle — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Division and Multiplication Together
slides.storyContext: The budget has 12,000. It's split equally among 4 committees. Each gets 3,000. Then, each committee spends 2,000. How much is left total? Priya writes: (12,000 ÷ 4) - 2,000 = 3,000 - 2,000 = 1,000 per committee. Total left: 1,000 × 4 = 4,000.

example.solution: 24 ÷ 3 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16 (left to right for equal priority)

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide and multiply in the order they appear.

image.alt: Division and Multiplication Together — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: The Final Calculation
slides.storyContext: Principal asks: If we spend 3,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 today and get a 10% discount on food, what's the final cost? Priya calculates: 10% of 3,000 = 300. So (3,000 - 300) + 2,000 + 1,500 = 2,700 + 2,000 + 1,500 = 6,200.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use expressions to calculate real budgets with discounts.

image.alt: The Final Calculation — Arithmetic Expressions

slides.title: Arjun and Priya's Success
slides.storyContext: The festival is a hit! Arjun and Priya present the final report: Total spent = 6,200. Budget left = 800. The principal smiles. You solved this with perfect arithmetic!

points.label: Arithmetic Mastery
points.text: Use BODMAS, brackets, and careful order to solve real problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arithmetic expressions solve real-world budgets and plans.

image.alt: Arjun and Priya's Success — Arithmetic Expressions

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Explore Geometry
hook: Discover points, lines, and angles in the world around you with Arjun and Priya!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious builder who sees shapes in buildings

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A geometry expert explaining the world's structure

slides.title: A Tiny Dot and Endless Lines
slides.storyContext: Walking through Delhi, Arjun spots a dusty ground. He draws a single dot with his finger. What's that? he asks. Priya replies: That's a point - it has no length, width, or height. It's just a location! Then she draws a line through it. A line goes on forever in both directions!
slides.inSimpleWords: A point is a tiny location. A line goes forever.

image.alt: A Tiny Dot and Endless Lines — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Line Segments and Rays
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: A line segment is part of a line - it has two endpoints. Like the edge of a door. She draws a segment. A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. Like a laser beam!

points.label: Segments vs. Rays
points.text: Line segment: two endpoints (finite). Ray: one endpoint, goes forever in one direction.

example.problem: Name the line segment between points A and B.
example.solution: Line segment AB (or BA)

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends. A ray has one end.

image.alt: Line Segments and Rays — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Where Lines Meet — Angles
slides.storyContext: They look at a street corner where two roads meet. That's an angle! says Priya, pointing. Two rays meeting at a point, called the vertex. The space between them is the angle. She shows Arjun with her arms. 90 degrees is a right angle - like a corner of a book!

points.label: Angle Basics
points.text: Two rays from one point form an angle. The point is the vertex. Angles measured in degrees. 90° = right angle.

example.problem: What's the angle at the corner of a square book?
example.solution: 90 degrees (right angle)

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure the space between two rays.

image.alt: Where Lines Meet — Angles — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Parallel Lines Never Meet
slides.storyContext: Walking past railway tracks, Arjun points: Look - two lines that never meet! Priya nods: These are parallel lines. They stay the same distance apart forever. Watch how the electricity wires above do the same thing!

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Lines that never meet, no matter how far they extend. Stay the same distance apart.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines never cross or touch.

image.alt: Parallel Lines Never Meet — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Intersecting Lines and Angles
slides.storyContext: Two roads cross in an X shape. When lines intersect, Priya explains, they create 4 angles. Opposite angles are equal! She measures with a protractor. This angle is 60 degrees. The opposite is also 60 degrees!

points.label: Vertical Angles
points.text: When two lines cross, opposite angles are equal.

example.problem: If one angle is 70°, what's the opposite angle?
example.solution: Also 70° (vertical angles are equal)

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles at intersections are always equal.

image.alt: Intersecting Lines and Angles — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Acute, Right, and Obtuse
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun three angles: a sharp one (acute), a square corner (right), and a wide one (obtuse). An acute angle is less than 90°. A right angle is exactly 90°. An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°. Arjun laughs. Like faces - happy (acute), neutral (right), surprised (obtuse)!

points.label: Angle Types
points.text: Acute: < 90°. Right: = 90°. Obtuse: > 90° but < 180°. Straight: = 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are sharp, square, or wide.

image.alt: Acute, Right, and Obtuse — A Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: The Geometry All Around
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Arjun and Priya look at the city skyline - dots of lights, lines of streets, angles of buildings. Geometry is everywhere! says Arjun. Priya smiles. Yes. Points, lines, and angles build our world.

points.label: Geometry Fundamentals
points.text: Points, lines, segments, rays, angles, and their relationships form the foundation of all shapes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry is the study of space, points, and shapes.

image.alt: The Geometry All Around — A Peek Beyond the Point

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Navigate City Streets
hook: Discover how parallel and intersecting lines shape our cities!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious navigator mapping city patterns

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A geometry expert explaining street designs

slides.title: A Grid of Streets
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya look at a city map. Notice the pattern? says Priya. North-South streets run parallel - they never meet. East-West streets also run parallel. But North-South and East-West streets intersect at right angles! Arjun traces with his finger. Like a giant grid!
slides.inSimpleWords: Cities are laid out with parallel and intersecting streets.

image.alt: A Grid of Streets — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Parallel Lines — Always the Same Distance
slides.storyContext: They measure two North-South streets. These are always 500 meters apart, Priya explains, pointing at her map. No matter how far north or south you go, they stay 500 meters apart. That makes them parallel.

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Lines that never intersect and maintain constant distance apart. Symbol: ∥

example.problem: Are railway tracks parallel?
example.solution: Yes, they maintain equal distance and never meet

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines stay the same distance forever.

image.alt: Parallel Lines — Always the Same Distance — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Intersecting Lines and Their Angles
slides.storyContext: At a road crossing, Priya sets up a protractor. When two lines intersect, they create four angles. Watch! She points. The angle on the top-left and bottom-right are equal. The angle on the top-right and bottom-left are also equal! Arjun checks: 65° and 65°! And 115° and 115°!

points.label: Vertical Angles
points.text: When two lines intersect, opposite angles are equal.

example.problem: Two lines intersect. One angle is 45°. Find the other three angles.
example.solution: Opposite angle: 45°. Adjacent angles: 135° each

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles at intersections are always equal.

image.alt: Intersecting Lines and Their Angles — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: A Transversal Cuts Through Parallel Lines
slides.storyContext: Priya draws three lines on paper: two parallel horizontal lines, and one diagonal line cutting through both. This diagonal is a transversal - it intersects both parallel lines! Arjun asks: Do the angles match? Priya smiles. Yes! Corresponding angles are equal!

points.label: Transversal Angles
points.text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines: corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: A transversal cuts parallel lines at matching angles.

image.alt: A Transversal Cuts Through Parallel Lines — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Finding Angles with a Transversal
slides.storyContext: A slanted power line (transversal) crosses two parallel streets. Priya measures one angle: 70°. By the transversal property, the corresponding angle at the other street is also 70°. And the alternate angle is 70° too! Arjun nods. Geometry is predictable!

points.label: Angle Relationships
points.text: Corresponding angles are equal. Alternate interior angles are equal. Co-interior angles sum to 180°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines at 60°. What's the alternate interior angle?
example.solution: Also 60° (alternate angles are equal)

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles match when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.

image.alt: Finding Angles with a Transversal — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: Perpendicular Lines — The 90-Degree Special
slides.storyContext: They spot a lamp post standing straight up, crossing a horizontal cable. These lines are perpendicular, says Priya. They intersect at exactly 90 degrees. Arjun checks with a square corner. Perfect! Symbol is ⊥.

points.label: Perpendicular Lines
points.text: Lines that intersect at 90 degrees. Symbol: ⊥

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular lines cross at right angles (90°).

image.alt: Perpendicular Lines — The 90-Degree Special — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

slides.title: City Geometry Unlocked
slides.storyContext: Walking home through the planned city streets, Arjun points out parallel lines, intersections, and perpendicular lamp posts. Our city is built on geometry! he says. Priya agrees. And now you can read it all!

points.label: Summary
points.text: Parallel lines stay apart. Intersecting lines cross. Transversals create angle relationships. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel and intersecting lines design cities.

image.alt: City Geometry Unlocked — Parallel and Intersecting Lines

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Share a Pizza
hook: Learn fractions by sharing pizza and sweets with Arjun and Priya!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A pizza-loving 12-year-old learning to share fairly

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A fair-minded math expert

slides.title: A Pizza Divided
slides.storyContext: At a cafe, Arjun and Priya order a pizza cut into 8 equal slices. Arjun takes 3 slices. That's 3/8 of the pizza, says Priya. The top number tells us how many parts we have. The bottom number tells us how many equal parts the whole pizza is cut into.
slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows a part of a whole.

image.alt: A Pizza Divided — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: In 3/8, the 3 is the numerator - the number on top, showing how many parts we have. The 8 is the denominator - the number on bottom, showing the total parts. She draws a pizza diagram. If we have 3/8, we're missing 5/8. Together: 3/8 + 5/8 = 8/8 = 1 whole pizza!

points.label: Parts of a Fraction
points.text: Numerator (top): parts we have. Denominator (bottom): total parts the whole is divided into.

example.problem: In 5/12, what do 5 and 12 represent?
example.solution: 5 = parts we have. 12 = total parts in the whole

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = parts we have. Bottom number = total parts.

image.alt: Numerator and Denominator — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
slides.storyContext: Priya has 2/8 of a barfi. Arjun has 3/8. Let's combine them! says Priya. 2/8 + 3/8: we just add the top numbers and keep the bottom. 2 + 3 = 5, so we get 5/8.

points.label: Adding Fractions
points.text: If denominators are the same, add numerators: a/c + b/c = (a+b)/c

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions by adding tops if bottoms match.

image.alt: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator) — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Finding Common Denominators
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 1/2 of a gulab jamun. Priya has 1/3. Can we add these? asks Arjun. Priya thinks. 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Now they have the same bottom! 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6! Arjun's eyes light up. We found a common denominator!

points.label: Common Denominators
points.text: Rewrite fractions so they have the same denominator. Find the LCM of the denominators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Make bottoms the same before adding fractions.

image.alt: Finding Common Denominators — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Multiplying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: What's 1/2 of 2/3 of a chocolate bar? Priya multiplies: 1/2 x 2/3: multiply tops and bottoms. (1x2)/(2x3) = 2/6 = 1/3. She shades a bar to show. Yes, exactly 1/3 of a bar!

points.label: Multiplying Fractions
points.text: (a/b) x (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d). Multiply tops and bottoms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions by multiplying tops and bottoms.

image.alt: Multiplying Fractions — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya draws two pizzas: one cut into 4 slices with 2 shaded, another cut into 8 slices with 4 shaded. Look! 2/4 and 4/8 show the same amount - they're equivalent fractions! Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

points.label: Equivalent Fractions
points.text: 2/4 = 4/8 = 1/2. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same amount can be written as different fractions.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Pizza Math Mastered
slides.storyContext: Walking home, Arjun and Priya review: Fractions have numerators and denominators. We add by finding common bottoms. We multiply by multiplying tops and bottoms. Equivalent fractions show the same parts differently. Arjun smiles. Now I can split anything fairly!

points.label: Fraction Mastery
points.text: Understand parts and wholes. Add with common denominators. Multiply numerators and denominators. Simplify to equivalent fractions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are parts of wholes, shared and calculated.

image.alt: Pizza Math Mastered — Working with Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Discover Number Magic
hook: Explore factors, multiples, and prime numbers in this fun number adventure!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: An enthusiastic puzzle-solver discovering patterns

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A number theorist revealing number secrets

slides.title: What Divides Into 12?
slides.storyContext: At home, Arjun arranges 12 candies in rows. I can make 2 rows of 6, or 3 rows of 4, or 4 rows of 3! Priya nods. Those are factors of 12 - numbers that divide evenly into 12. Factors of 12 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.
slides.inSimpleWords: Factors divide evenly into a number.

image.alt: What Divides Into 12? — Number Play

slides.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun cards with numbers: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Like 7 - only 1 and 7 divide into it! She shows another: 12 has many factors. It's composite. Arjun asks: Is 1 prime? Priya shakes her head. 1 is special - neither prime nor composite.

points.label: Prime vs. Composite
points.text: Prime: exactly 2 factors (1 and itself). Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Composite: more than 2 factors. Example: 12.

example.problem: Is 9 prime or composite?
example.solution: Composite. Factors: 1, 3, 9

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers only divide by 1 and themselves.

image.alt: Prime and Composite Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples — Skip Counting
slides.storyContext: Priya counts: Multiples of 3 are: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18... She hops on a number line. Each time, I skip by 3. These are all multiples of 3 - they all have 3 as a factor!

points.label: Multiples
points.text: Multiples of n: n×1, n×2, n×3... Example: multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20...

example.problem: List the first 5 multiples of 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get by skip-counting.

image.alt: Multiples — Skip Counting — Number Play

slides.title: GCD — Finding the Greatest Common Factor
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 12 marbles, Priya has 18. They want to divide them into equal piles with no leftovers. What's the largest pile size that works for both? asks Arjun. Priya lists: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The greatest common factor is 6! They make 2 piles of 6 marbles each.

points.label: GCD (Greatest Common Divisor)
points.text: The largest number that divides evenly into two numbers. GCD(12, 18) = 6

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the largest number dividing both.

image.alt: GCD — Finding the Greatest Common Factor — Number Play

slides.title: LCM — Finding the Least Common Multiple
slides.storyContext: Arjun's bus comes every 4 minutes. Priya's comes every 6 minutes. When will both buses arrive together? Priya calculates: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24... The least common multiple is 12. Both buses arrive together every 12 minutes!

points.label: LCM (Least Common Multiple)
points.text: The smallest number that is a multiple of both. LCM(4, 6) = 12

example.problem: Find LCM(5, 8)

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM is the smallest number both divide into.

image.alt: LCM — Finding the Least Common Multiple — Number Play

slides.title: Divisibility Rules Make It Faster
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches shortcuts: A number is divisible by 2 if it's even. By 3 if its digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5 if it ends in 0 or 5. By 10 if it ends in 0. She checks 135: 1+3+5=9, which is divisible by 3, so 135 is too! Arjun tries 156: 1+5+6=12, divisible by 3! 156 ÷ 3 = 52!

points.label: Divisibility Shortcuts
points.text: Divisible by 2: even. By 3: digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0/5. By 10: ends in 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use shortcuts to check if numbers divide evenly.

image.alt: Divisibility Rules Make It Faster — Number Play

slides.title: The World of Number Patterns
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya review their number adventure: factors, primes, composites, multiples, GCD, LCM. Numbers have hidden patterns! says Arjun. Priya smiles. Yes. And now you can see them all.

points.label: Number Fundamentals
points.text: Factors divide into numbers. Primes have 2 factors. Multiples are skip-counted. GCD and LCM solve shared problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number patterns connect factors, multiples, and primes.

image.alt: The World of Number Patterns — Number Play

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya's Garden Adventure
hook: Discover how plants make their own food in this green story!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious gardener wondering how plants grow

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A plant scientist explaining photosynthesis

slides.title: Why Do Plants Need Roots?
slides.storyContext: In their school garden, Arjun plants a seed. Priya says: The roots do two important jobs. First, they hold the plant in soil so it doesn't tip over. Second, they absorb water and minerals from the soil - that's nutrition! Arjun digs carefully. So roots are like a food pipeline?
slides.inSimpleWords: Roots absorb water and minerals for plant nutrition.

image.alt: Why Do Plants Need Roots? — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Green Power — Photosynthesis
slides.storyContext: Priya points at the green leaves. Inside these leaves, plants have a special power! They trap sunlight and use it to make food from water and air. It's called photosynthesis! She writes: Sunlight + Water + Carbon Dioxide = Glucose (sugar) + Oxygen.

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: Plants make glucose (food) using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. They release oxygen as a bonus!

example.problem: What three things does a plant need for photosynthesis?
example.solution: Sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide (from air)

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants make food using sun, water, and air.

image.alt: Green Power — Photosynthesis — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Chlorophyll — The Green Pigment
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: Why are leaves green? Priya smiles. Because of chlorophyll - a green pigment inside leaf cells. It captures sunlight! She holds up a leaf to the sun. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, but reflects green light. That's why it looks green to us!

points.label: Chlorophyll
points.text: Green pigment in plant cells that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. It absorbs red/blue light and reflects green.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps sunlight.

image.alt: Chlorophyll — The Green Pigment — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Heterotrophic Plants — Dodder and Mistletoe
slides.storyContext: Priya points at a vine wrapping around a tree. Not all plants are green! Some, like dodder, can't make their own food. They're parasites - they steal nutrients from other plants! Arjun shivers. That's mean! Priya nods. It's nature's strategy. Most plants are autotrophs and make their own food. A few are parasites.

points.label: Autotrophs vs. Parasites
points.text: Autotrophs (like most plants) make their own food. Parasites (like dodder) steal food from host plants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most plants make food. Some steal it from other plants.

image.alt: Heterotrophic Plants — Dodder and Mistletoe — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Minerals Plants Need
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a withered plant next to a healthy one. This plant had water but lacked nutrients. Plants need: nitrogen (for growth), phosphorus (for roots and flowers), potassium (for strength). She sprinkles fertilizer on the soil. Now it has all the minerals it needs!

points.label: Essential Minerals
points.text: Nitrogen: growth. Phosphorus: roots/flowers. Potassium: strength. Plants absorb these through roots.

example.problem: Why do farmers add fertilizer to soil?
example.solution: To provide nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium plants need for healthy growth

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need minerals from soil for good health.

image.alt: Minerals Plants Need — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Transpiration — Plants Release Water
slides.storyContext: Arjun covers a plant with a plastic bag. Within hours, water droplets appear inside. Where did that come from? he asks. Priya explains: Plants absorb more water than they use. They release extra water vapor through leaves - that's transpiration. The bag traps it, showing us!

points.label: Transpiration
points.text: Plants release water vapor through leaves. It's like plant sweating on a hot day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants release water through leaves as vapor.

image.alt: Transpiration — Plants Release Water — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: The Complete Plant Story
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya sit under a mango tree. Roots absorb water and minerals. Leaves capture sunlight and make food. Plants release oxygen for us to breathe and water for the ecosystem. Everything is connected! says Priya. Arjun smiles. Plants are farmers of sunlight!

points.label: Plant Nutrition Summary
points.text: Roots absorb water/minerals. Photosynthesis makes food. Chlorophyll captures light. Plants are autotrophs except parasites.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants are self-feeding organisms using sun energy.

image.alt: The Complete Plant Story — Nutrition in Plants

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya Explore Food Chains
hook: Follow how animals eat and digest food in this natural story!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious observer of animal behavior

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: An animal nutrition expert

slides.title: Who Eats Whom?
slides.storyContext: At a wildlife sanctuary, Arjun watches a deer eating grass, then a tiger stalking the deer. Nature's food chain! says Priya. Grass gets energy from the sun. Deer eats grass. Tiger eats deer. Energy flows from one to the next.
slides.inSimpleWords: Energy moves through food chains: plants to herbivores to carnivores.

image.alt: Who Eats Whom? — Nutrition in Animals

slides.title: Herbivores, Carnivores, and Omnivores
slides.storyContext: Priya points: Herbivores like deer eat only plants. Carnivores like tigers eat only meat. Omnivores like bears eat plants AND meat. Arjun asks: Which are humans? Priya smiles. Humans are omnivores - we eat both!

points.label: Animal Types
points.text: Herbivores: plants. Carnivores: meat. Omnivores: both. Decomposers: dead matter (bacteria, fungi).

example.problem: Is a cow a herbivore or omnivore?
example.solution: Herbivore - cows eat only grass and plants

slides.inSimpleWords: Animals eat plants, meat, or both.

image.alt: Herbivores, Carnivores, and Omnivores — Nutrition in Animals

slides.title: The Digestive System — Breaking Down Food
slides.storyContext: Priya draws the digestive system: Food enters the mouth, goes down the esophagus, enters the stomach where it's mixed with acids and churned, then moves to the small intestine where nutrients are absorbed, and finally exits as waste. Arjun follows along. It's a long journey!

points.label: Digestive Journey
points.text: Mouth → Esophagus → Stomach (churning + acids) → Small intestine (nutrient absorption) → Large intestine → Excretion

example.problem: Where are nutrients absorbed in the digestive system?
example.solution: In the small intestine

slides.inSimpleWords: Digestive system breaks food into usable nutrients.

image.alt: The Digestive System — Breaking Down Food — Nutrition in Animals

slides.title: Teeth Built for the Job
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at different animal skulls. Herbivores have flat molars for grinding plants. Carnivores have sharp canines for tearing meat. Omnivores have both! Priya nods. Evolution shaped teeth for diet!

points.label: Teeth Adaptation
points.text: Incisors: cutting. Canines: tearing. Molars: grinding. Each tooth type suits different diets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Teeth shape matches what an animal eats.

image.alt: Teeth Built for the Job — Nutrition in Animals

slides.title: Stomach and Intestines — Different Sizes
slides.storyContext: Priya compares: Herbivores like cows have long intestines to digest tough plant fiber - takes a long time! Carnivores like tigers have short intestines because meat is easier to digest. Their stomachs are huge to hold big meals!

points.label: Digestive Adaptations
points.text: Herbivores: long intestines for fiber. Carnivores: short intestines, large stomachs. Each adapted to diet.

example.problem: Why do herbivores need longer intestines?
example.solution: Plant fiber needs more time and length to be broken down and nutrients absorbed

slides.inSimpleWords: Intestine length matches how easy food is to digest.

image.alt: Stomach and Intestines — Different Sizes — Nutrition in Animals

slides.title: Decomposers Close the Loop
slides.storyContext: Arjun spots fungi on a dead log. Dead things rot, he observes. Priya explains: Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down dead matter and return nutrients to soil. Nothing is wasted in nature! A new plant sprouts from the enriched soil. The cycle continues!

points.label: Decomposers
points.text: Bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms, returning nutrients to soil for plants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Decomposers recycle dead matter into soil nutrients.

image.alt: Decomposers Close the Loop — Nutrition in Animals

slides.title: The Circle of Life
slides.storyContext: Walking through the sanctuary, Arjun and Priya see everything connected: plants make food, herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat herbivores, decomposers recycle the dead. It's one big system! says Arjun. Priya nods. Every creature has a role.

points.label: Nutrition in Animals
points.text: Food chains link herbivores, carnivores, omnivores. Digestive systems extract nutrients. Decomposers recycle. Nature cycles endlessly.

slides.inSimpleWords: All animals depend on food chains and nutrients.

image.alt: The Circle of Life — Nutrition in Animals

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya Understand Temperature and Heat
hook: Explore how heat transfers and changes everything around us!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious learner feeling heat in everyday life

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A heat scientist explaining thermal energy

slides.title: Heat vs. Temperature — Not the Same!
slides.storyContext: On a hot day, Arjun complains: It's so hot! Priya says: Temperature is what a thermometer measures - how fast molecules move. Heat is the energy that flows from hot to cold. They're different! She holds a cup of hot chai and a cup of cold water. The chai has higher temperature. But it has less heat energy than a swimming pool because it's smaller!
slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature measures hotness. Heat is thermal energy flow.

image.alt: Heat vs. Temperature — Not the Same! — Heat

slides.title: How Heat Transfers — Conduction
slides.storyContext: Priya places a metal spoon in hot tea. Soon the spoon handle gets hot too! That's conduction - heat traveling through a solid without it moving. She waits. Metals are good conductors. Wood is not - that's why wooden handles don't burn! Arjun touches cautiously. Science protects us!

points.label: Conduction
points.text: Heat travels through solid materials. Good conductors: metals. Poor conductors: wood, plastic, air.

example.problem: Why don't you burn your hand on a wooden spoon in hot water?
example.solution: Wood is a poor conductor - heat transfers very slowly through it

slides.inSimpleWords: Conduction moves heat through solids.

image.alt: How Heat Transfers — Conduction — Heat

slides.title: How Heat Transfers — Convection
slides.storyContext: Priya boils water. Watch the bubbles rise! She points. Hot water becomes less dense and rises. Cold water sinks. This circular motion is convection - how heat travels in liquids and gases. That's how your room gets warm from a heater in the corner!

points.label: Convection
points.text: Hot fluids (liquid/gas) rise. Cold fluids sink. Creates circular currents. Example: air in a room from a heater.

example.problem: How does a heater warm a room?
example.solution: Hot air rises and circulates (convection), spreading warmth throughout

slides.inSimpleWords: Convection moves heat through fluids by circulation.

image.alt: How Heat Transfers — Convection — Heat

slides.title: How Heat Transfers — Radiation
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands in sunlight. The sun warms me, but there's no air or solid between us! Priya explains: That's radiation - heat travels as waves through empty space. The sun's rays reach Earth directly. No medium needed!, She points at a lamp. Infrared heat lamps use radiation too.

points.label: Radiation
points.text: Heat travels as electromagnetic waves. Works through empty space. Sun's rays, heat lamps, fire.

slides.inSimpleWords: Radiation sends heat through empty space as waves.

image.alt: How Heat Transfers — Radiation — Heat

slides.title: Insulation Stops Heat Loss
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a thermos flask. To keep tea hot, we use insulation - materials that prevent heat loss. The flask has air gaps between layers because air is a poor conductor. So heat stays trapped inside! She pours hot tea into a normal cup and a thermos. Hours later, the thermos is still warm. That's insulation working!

points.label: Insulation
points.text: Materials or air gaps that prevent heat transfer. Traps heat inside. Examples: thermos, wool, foam.

example.problem: Why do animals have fur?
example.solution: Fur insulates - it traps air, preventing body heat from escaping

slides.inSimpleWords: Insulation prevents heat from leaving objects.

image.alt: Insulation Stops Heat Loss — Heat

slides.title: Heat Changes Matter — Melting and Boiling
slides.storyContext: Priya heats ice. At 0 degrees C, ice melts to water - the solid becomes liquid. At 100 degrees C, water boils to steam - the liquid becomes gas. Arjun watches the transformations. Heat makes solids liquid, and liquids gas!

points.label: State Changes
points.text: Melting (solid→liquid at 0°C). Boiling (liquid→gas at 100°C). Reverse: freezing and condensation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat makes solids liquid, liquids gaseous.

image.alt: Heat Changes Matter — Melting and Boiling — Heat

slides.title: Heat Powers Our World
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya sit by a fire. Heat transfers by conduction, convection, and radiation. It changes matter, warms homes, cooks food, powers machines. Heat is everywhere! says Priya. Arjun nods. And now I understand it all!

points.label: Heat Mastery
points.text: Temperature vs. heat. Three transfer methods. Conduction through solids. Convection in fluids. Radiation through space. Insulation stops loss.

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat is thermal energy that moves and changes everything.

image.alt: Heat Powers Our World — Heat

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya's Chemistry Kitchen
hook: Discover acids, bases, and salts in your own kitchen!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious kitchen chemist experimenting safely

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A chemistry expert explaining reactions

slides.title: Taste Testing with the pH Scale
slides.storyContext: Priya sets up containers: lemon juice, baking soda solution, table salt water. Let's understand acids and bases! She uses litmus paper - red for acids, blue for bases. Lemon juice turns red: That's acidic! Baking soda turns blue: That's basic or alkaline! Salt water stays neutral. Arjun, everything has a pH!
slides.inSimpleWords: pH scale measures if something is acidic, basic, or neutral.

image.alt: Taste Testing with the pH Scale — Acids Bases and Salts

slides.title: What Are Acids?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: Acids have a sour taste and turn litmus red. Lemon juice, vinegar, and your stomach acid are all acidic! She shows examples: Citric acid (in citrus), acetic acid (in vinegar), hydrochloric acid (in stomachs). Acids have pH less than 7 on the pH scale.

points.label: Acids
points.text: Sour taste. Turn litmus red. pH < 7. Examples: lemon, vinegar, stomach acid.

example.problem: Is apple juice acidic or basic?
example.solution: Acidic - apples contain citric acid, sour taste

slides.inSimpleWords: Acids are sour and turn red litmus paper.

image.alt: What Are Acids? — Acids Bases and Salts

slides.title: What Are Bases?
slides.storyContext: Priya shows soap and baking soda. These are basic - also called alkaline. They have a bitter taste, feel slippery, and turn litmus blue. Bases have pH greater than 7. Arjun asks: Why is soap slippery? Priya smiles. That's a property of bases!

points.label: Bases
points.text: Bitter taste. Slippery feel. Turn litmus blue. pH > 7. Examples: soap, baking soda, ammonia.

example.problem: Why do you use soap (a base) to wash hands?
example.solution: Bases break down and remove oils, making washing effective

slides.inSimpleWords: Bases are bitter, slippery, and turn blue litmus paper.

image.alt: What Are Bases? — Acids Bases and Salts

slides.title: Neutralization — Acid + Base = Salt + Water
slides.storyContext: Priya pours lemon juice (acid) into baking soda (base). Fizz! It reacts. When acids and bases meet, they neutralize each other! She lets it settle. The result is salt and water - neutral pH = 7. Arjun tastes: Not sour anymore, not bitter either!

points.label: Neutralization
points.text: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. Example: lemon juice + baking soda → sodium citrate (salt) + water

slides.inSimpleWords: Acids and bases neutralize each other to make salts.

image.alt: Neutralization — Acid + Base = Salt + Water — Acids Bases and Salts

slides.title: Real-World Neutralization
slides.storyContext: Arjun has heartburn. Priya explains: Your stomach produces too much acid. A base like milk of magnesia neutralizes it! She shows another: Ant stings inject formic acid. Baking soda paste neutralizes it! Arjun nods. Neutralization heals!

points.label: Medical Applications
points.text: Antacids (bases) neutralize stomach acid. Baking soda neutralizes stings and burns.

example.problem: How does baking soda help an ant sting?
example.solution: Baking soda (base) neutralizes formic acid (from the ant), reducing pain

slides.inSimpleWords: Neutralization helps treat acid problems in body.

image.alt: Real-World Neutralization — Acids Bases and Salts

slides.title: What Are Salts?
slides.storyContext: Priya shows table salt. This is sodium chloride - a salt. Salts form when acids and bases neutralize. Most salts are white crystals and taste salty! Arjun asks: Are all salts from acid-base reactions? Priya nods. Yes! And salts are essential - your body needs them!

points.label: Salts
points.text: Form from acid-base neutralization. Usually white crystals. Taste salty. Essential for body (sodium, chloride in sweat).

slides.inSimpleWords: Salts form when acids meet bases.

image.alt: What Are Salts? — Acids Bases and Salts

slides.title: Chemistry in the Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun clean up their kitchen experiment. Acids and bases are all around us - in food, cleaning, medicine. And when they meet, they neutralize to form salts. Chemistry is in everything! says Priya. Arjun grins. The kitchen is a chemistry lab!

points.label: Acids, Bases, Salts
points.text: Acids: sour, pH < 7, red litmus. Bases: bitter, slippery, pH > 7, blue litmus. Salts: neutral, formed from neutralization.

slides.inSimpleWords: Acids, bases, and salts are everyday chemistry.

image.alt: Chemistry in the Kitchen — Acids Bases and Salts

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya's Transformation Lab
hook: Learn the difference between physical and chemical changes!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: An experimenter noticing how things change

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A change scientist explaining transformations

slides.title: Breaking Ice — What Happens?
slides.storyContext: Arjun drops an ice cube into a cup. It melts to water, then he heats it to steam. It changed forms! he says. Priya nods. But it's still H2O - water molecules. The substance didn't change, just its physical state. That's a physical change!
slides.inSimpleWords: Physical changes alter appearance but not substance.

image.alt: Breaking Ice — What Happens? — Physical and Chemical Changes

slides.title: Physical Changes — Reversible Transformations
slides.storyContext: Priya demonstrates: Melting ice (solid→liquid), boiling water (liquid→gas), cutting paper, mixing salt and sand - these are all physical changes. You can reverse most of them! Freeze water to ice again. Condense steam back to water. Arjun tries mixing salt and sand. I can separate them with a magnet or sieve - the materials stay the same!

points.label: Physical Changes
points.text: Change shape, size, or state. No new substance forms. Reversible. Examples: melting, freezing, cutting, mixing.

example.problem: Is tearing paper a physical change?
example.solution: Yes - the paper's size/shape changed, but it's still paper

slides.inSimpleWords: Physical changes are reversible and don't create new materials.

image.alt: Physical Changes — Reversible Transformations — Physical and Chemical Changes

slides.title: Chemical Changes — New Substances Form
slides.storyContext: Priya lights a candle. Watch this! Wax melts (physical), then burns (chemical). Burning combines wax with oxygen, creating carbon dioxide and water vapor - completely new substances! You can't turn them back into wax. That's a chemical change!

points.label: Chemical Changes
points.text: New substances form. Often irreversible. Examples: burning, rusting, digestion, cooking, fermentation.

example.problem: Is cooking an egg a chemical change?
example.solution: Yes - heat transforms protein structure, creating new substances (cooked egg), can't be reversed

slides.inSimpleWords: Chemical changes create new substances and are usually irreversible.

image.alt: Chemical Changes — New Substances Form — Physical and Chemical Changes

slides.title: Signs of Chemical Changes
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun clues: Heat released (burning), color change (rusting: red to brown), gas bubbles (vinegar + baking soda), smell change (cooking), light produced (sparkler). She demonstrates each. These signs tell us a chemical change happened!

points.label: Chemical Change Signs
points.text: Heat released/absorbed. Color change. Gas bubbles. Odor change. Light production. Explosion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chemical changes show heat, color, gas, smell, or light.

image.alt: Signs of Chemical Changes — Physical and Chemical Changes

slides.title: Rusting — A Slow Chemical Change
slides.storyContext: Priya shows an iron nail turning orange-brown. This is rust - iron oxidizing when it meets oxygen and water. It's a chemical change. The iron becomes iron oxide - a new substance! Unlike melting wax, you can't reverse rust easily. That's why we paint metal to protect it!

points.label: Oxidation (Rusting)
points.text: Iron + Oxygen + Water → Iron Oxide (rust). Irreversible chemical change. Prevents by painting or coating.

example.problem: How do you prevent iron from rusting?
example.solution: Paint, coat with oil, or use stainless steel - prevents contact with oxygen and water

slides.inSimpleWords: Rust is iron chemically combining with oxygen.

image.alt: Rusting — A Slow Chemical Change — Physical and Chemical Changes

slides.title: Digestion — A Series of Chemical Changes
slides.storyContext: Arjun eats an apple. Priya explains: Your saliva starts breaking down food (chemical change). Your stomach acid and enzymes continue. Nutrients are created for your body to absorb. That's why you can't un-digest food - chemical changes made it become different molecules!

points.label: Digestion
points.text: Series of chemical reactions. Food broken into absorbable nutrients. Irreversible. Enzymes and acids essential.

slides.inSimpleWords: Digestion breaks food into new nutrients via chemistry.

image.alt: Digestion — A Series of Chemical Changes — Physical and Chemical Changes

slides.title: Changes Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya review: Physical changes alter appearance but substance stays the same - reversible. Chemical changes create new substances - usually irreversible. From burning to rusting to cooking to digestion, the world is full of transformations! Priya smiles. Now you know the difference!

points.label: Summary
points.text: Physical: reversible, same substance. Chemical: irreversible, new substance. Signs: heat, color, gas, smell, light.

slides.inSimpleWords: Physical changes are reversible. Chemical changes are usually permanent.

image.alt: Changes Everywhere — Physical and Chemical Changes

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya Discover Breathing and Energy
hook: Explore how all living things breathe and get energy!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious athlete noticing his breathing

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A biology expert explaining cellular respiration

slides.title: Why Do We Breathe?
slides.storyContext: After running, Arjun breathes heavily. Why am I breathing so fast? Priya explains: Your cells need oxygen to release energy from food. That process is respiration. It's not just breathing - breathing is how you get oxygen in. Respiration happens inside every cell!
slides.inSimpleWords: Breathing brings oxygen. Respiration releases energy from food.

image.alt: Why Do We Breathe? — Respiration in Organisms

slides.title: Aerobic Respiration — With Oxygen
slides.storyContext: Priya writes an equation: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon Dioxide + Water + Energy (ATP). With oxygen, cells completely break down glucose. This releases lots of energy! Your muscles, brain, everything uses this energy to function. That's aerobic respiration - the main way we get energy.

points.label: Aerobic Respiration
points.text: Glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O + Energy. Happens in mitochondria. Most efficient way to get energy.

example.problem: What do your cells produce when they use oxygen?
example.solution: Carbon dioxide and water (plus energy)

slides.inSimpleWords: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen to release lots of energy.

image.alt: Aerobic Respiration — With Oxygen — Respiration in Organisms

slides.title: Anaerobic Respiration — Without Oxygen
slides.storyContext: During a sprint, Arjun's muscles work so hard they run low on oxygen. Your muscles switch to anaerobic respiration! says Priya. They break down glucose WITHOUT oxygen - but it's less efficient. You feel tired and your muscles ache because lactic acid builds up. That's why athletes pant after sprinting - they're repaying their oxygen debt!

points.label: Anaerobic Respiration
points.text: Glucose → Lactic acid + Some energy (in animals). Happens when oxygen is low. Less efficient. Causes muscle fatigue.

example.problem: Why do your muscles ache after intense exercise?
example.solution: Lactic acid buildup from anaerobic respiration in low-oxygen conditions

slides.inSimpleWords: Anaerobic respiration works without oxygen but less efficiently.

image.alt: Anaerobic Respiration — Without Oxygen — Respiration in Organisms

slides.title: Breathing in Humans — the Respiratory System
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a lung diagram. Air enters your nose, travels down the trachea, splits into bronchi into both lungs. Inside tiny air sacs called alveoli, oxygen enters your blood! CO2 leaves your blood to be exhaled. Arjun follows. It's a gas exchange!

points.label: Breathing Process
points.text: Nose → Trachea → Bronchi → Lungs → Alveoli. Oxygen diffuses into blood. CO2 diffuses out. Diaphragm contracts to pull air in.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lungs exchange oxygen for carbon dioxide.

image.alt: Breathing in Humans — the Respiratory System — Respiration in Organisms

slides.title: Respiration in Plants
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a potted plant. Plants photosynthesize during the day (make glucose and oxygen). But at night and all the time, they respire! They take in some oxygen and release CO2, just like us. They use glucose for growth and energy. Arjun asks: So plants both make and consume oxygen? Priya nods. They do!

points.label: Plant Respiration
points.text: Plants respire 24/7 using glucose for energy. Day: photosynthesis > respiration (net O2 release). Night: respiration only.

example.problem: Do plants need oxygen?
example.solution: Yes - roots especially need oxygen to respire and absorb water/minerals

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants also respire using oxygen and releasing CO2.

image.alt: Respiration in Plants — Respiration in Organisms

slides.title: Respiration in Other Organisms
slides.storyContext: Priya shows examples: Fish have gills to extract dissolved oxygen from water. Insects have tiny holes called spiracles for air. Earthworms breathe through their moist skin! Even bacteria respire - they're alive and need energy. Arjun smiles. Everyone needs to respire!

points.label: Respiration Variety
points.text: Fish: gills extract dissolved O2. Insects: spiracles. Earthworms: skin diffusion. Bacteria: aerobic/anaerobic. All release energy from food.

slides.inSimpleWords: All living things respire to get energy.

image.alt: Respiration in Other Organisms — Respiration in Organisms

slides.title: The Breath of Life
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya sit peacefully. Every breath, every moment, trillions of cells in your body are respiring - breaking down glucose with oxygen to release energy. Without respiration, there's no life. That's why breathing matters so much! says Priya. Arjun takes a deep breath. I'll never forget that!

points.label: Respiration Summary
points.text: Aerobic: glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O + Energy. Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid + less energy. All life respires.

slides.inSimpleWords: Respiration releases energy from food - it's how life works.

image.alt: The Breath of Life — Respiration in Organisms
